claim: OCLN is an integral tight junction protein recognized as part of epithelial and endothelial junctional complexes.
source: The integral tight junction (TJ) protein, occludin, is recognized as part of epithelial and endothelial junctional complexes (Furuse et al., 1996; Balda, 1996; Van Itallie and Anderson, 1997; McCarthy et al., 1996)
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature establishing OCLN as a tight junction protein

claim: OCLN is not required for tight junction assembly.
source: while not required for tight junction assembly (Saitou et al., 2000; Schulzke et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: OCLN regulates barrier properties.
source: recent data indicates occludin regulates barrier properties (Bolinger et al., 2016; Raleigh et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent published data

claim: In the embryonic cerebral cortex, OCLN is localized both at TJs between epithelial cells and at the apical surface of the ventricular zone (VZ) in the chick.
source: In the embryonic cerebral cortex, OCLN is localized both at TJs between epithelial cells and at the apical surface of the ventricular zone (VZ) in the chick (Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study in chick

claim: OCLN VZ expression was thought to be turned off around the neuroepithelial to radial glial cell (NE-to-RGC) transition at the onset of neurogenesis.
source: However, OCLN function in cortical development is virtually unexamined, as its VZ expression was thought to be turned off around the neuroepithelial to radial glial cell (NE-to-RGC) transition (embryonic day 11–12 (E11-E12) in the mouse), at the onset of neurogenesis (Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996; Sahara and O'Leary, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: A mouse model presumed to be an Ocln-null displayed postnatal growth retardation, brain calcification, and chronic inflammation.
source: A mouse model presumed to be an Ocln-null displayed postnatal growth retardation, brain calcification, and chronic inflammation.
evidence: Describes phenotypes observed in a previously generated mouse model

claim: Vascular endothelial TJs were still present in the Ocln mouse model.
source: However, vascular endothelial TJs were still present (Saitou et al., 2000), suggesting that Ocln is important for regulation of TJs but not for junction formation.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Mutations in JAM3 produce brain hemorrhage rather than congenital microcephaly and PMG.
source: Interestingly, mutations in other TJ protein-encoding genes such as JAM3 produce brain hemorrhage (Mochida et al., 2010) rather than the congenital microcephaly and PMG associated with the OCLN mutation phenotype in humans
evidence: Supported by citation to published study on JAM3 mutations

claim: Microcephaly can occur when expansion of the neural progenitor pool and subsequent generation of neurons is restricted.
source: Microcephaly, defined as head circumference of −2 standard deviations below the mean or smaller, can occur when expansion of the neural progenitor pool and subsequent generation of neurons is restricted (Kaindl et al., 2010; Manzini and Walsh, 2011; Mahmood et al., 2011; Thornton and Woods, 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Many genes causally linked to microcephaly have in common a role in regulating centrosome dynamics and mitotic spindle stabilization of progenitors in the ventricular neuroepithelium.
source: Among the extensive list of genes now causally linked to microcephaly, many have in common a role in regulating centrosome dynamics and mitotic spindle stabilization of progenitors in the ventricular neuroepithelium (Gilmore and Walsh, 2013; Faheem et al., 2015; Jayaraman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: At E10.5, mOCLN is localized to the neuroepithelial plasma membranes and at the centrosome during interphase.
source: At E10.5, mOCLN is localized to the neuroepithelial plasma membranes and at the centrosome during interphase (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1A

claim: At E10.5, mOCLN is localized to the centrosome during mitosis.
source: At E10.5, mOCLN is localized to the neuroepithelial plasma membranes and at the centrosome during interphase (Figure 1A) and mitosis (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: By E14.5, mOCLN was absent at the cell membrane.
source: By E14.5, mOCLN was absent at the cell membrane, in accordance with previous studies in which TJs are replaced by adherens junctions as neurogenesis begins (Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by observation in the study and citation to previous work

claim: mOCLN expression at both interphase and mitotic centrosomes persisted throughout and beyond the NE-to-RGC transition.
source: Surprisingly, mOCLN expression at both interphase and mitotic centrosomes persisted throughout and beyond the NE-to-RGC transition (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 1A and 1B

claim: Full-length mouse Ocln transcripts encode wild-type OCLN (mOCLN-FL) with four transmembrane domains, two extracellular loops with intracellular N- and C-termini.
source: Several mouse Ocln transcripts are annotated in the Ensembl database: (1) full-length transcripts with varying 3' and 5'UTR lengths, all encoding wild-type OCLN (mOCLN-FL) with four transmembrane domains, two extracellular loops with intracellular N- and C-termini
evidence: Based on annotation in Ensembl database

claim: One truncated mouse Ocln transcript (ENSMUST00000159459) lacks exons 2 and 3, resulting in the loss of the N-terminus and three of the four transmembrane domains (mOCLN-ΔN).
source: and (2) one truncated transcript (ENSMUST00000159459) lacking exons 2 and 3, resulting in the loss of the N-terminus and three of the four transmembrane domains (mOCLN-ΔN; UniProt E0CZ73) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on annotation in Ensembl database and UniProt, illustrated in Figure 1C

claim: mOCLN-FL resides in both membrane and soluble nuclear fractions.
source: Centrosomal localization of both isoforms was further supported by centrifugation-based subcellular fractionation of whole brain E12.5 lysates, which showed mOCLN-FL residing in both membrane and soluble nuclear fractions, with the latter fraction also containing centrosomal proteins γ-tubulin and phosphorylated-β-catenin (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Truncated mOCLN-ΔN could only be found in the soluble fraction.
source: In contrast, truncated mOCLN-ΔN could only be found in the soluble fraction.
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data

claim: Both OCLN isoforms localize to the centrosome while only mOCLN-FL localizes to the plasma membrane.
source: Together, these results indicate both OCLN isoforms localize to the centrosome while only mOCLN-FL localizes to the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from subcellular fractionation and immunohistochemistry data

claim: The truncated mOCLN-ΔN isoform is continually expressed during neurogenesis.
source: Furthermore, although mOCLN-FL expression is downregulated after the NE-to-RGC transition, the truncated mOCLN-ΔN isoform is continually expressed during neurogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from immunohistochemistry and fractionation data

claim: An Ocln loss-of-function mouse line was previously generated by excising exon three and was characterized as a homozygous null model.
source: An Ocln loss-of-function mouse line was previously generated by excising exon three and was characterized as a homozygous null model (Saitou et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: A shorter FL transcript in the mutant mouse has a frame shift predicting translation of a nonsense peptide with premature stop codon.
source: Using unique 5'UTR primers to distinguish between Ocln-FL and -ΔN transcripts, we noted a shorter FL transcript in the mutant mouse, whose PCR amplicon sequence revealed a frame shift predicting translation of a nonsense peptide with premature stop codon (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and sequencing data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: Both control and homozygous mutant mice have the presence of the shorter ΔN transcript lacking exons 2 and 3.
source: Moreover, we further noted in both control and homozygous mutant mice the presence of the shorter ΔN transcript lacking exons 2 and 3 which would not have been targeted for deletion in the mutant mouse.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data

claim: The ΔN transcript is translated to mOCLN-ΔN, a 32 kDa protein detectable by western blot using an antibody raised against the C-terminus of OCLN.
source: This transcript is translated to mOCLN-ΔN, a 32 kDa protein detectable by western blot using an antibody raised against the C-terminus of OCLN (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A,B

claim: mOCLN-FL was detected in wildtype mouse brain at E10.5, localized to both plasma membrane and centrosome.
source: Unlike the OclnΔN/ΔN mutant VZ progenitors, mOCLN-FL was detected in wildtype, Ocln+/+ mouse brain at E10.5, localized to both plasma membrane and centrosome, and was absent at the plasma membrane by E14.5 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C

claim: mOCLN-FL was absent at the plasma membrane by E14.5 in wildtype mouse brain.
source: Unlike the OclnΔN/ΔN mutant VZ progenitors, mOCLN-FL was detected in wildtype, Ocln+/+ mouse brain at E10.5, localized to both plasma membrane and centrosome, and was absent at the plasma membrane by E14.5 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Immunohistochemical labeling of mOCLN-FL was substantially reduced in VZ progenitor plasma membrane and centrosome at E12.5 in OclnΔN/ΔN mutants.
source: Immunohistochemical labeling of mOCLN-FL was substantially reduced in VZ progenitor plasma membrane and centrosome at E12.5 (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2C

claim: mOCLN-FL protein expression on Western blot in E12.5 Ocln +/+ total brain lysate remained strong, presumably due to the presence of tight junctions in the brain vasculature, choroid plexus and other epithelial and endothelial elements.
source: However, mOCLN-FL protein expression on Western blot in E12.5 Ocln +/+ total brain lysate remained strong, presumably due to the presence of tight junctions in the brain vasculature, choroid plexus and other epithelial and endothelial elements (Luissint et al., 2012; Kaur et al., 2016) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data and inference based on known OCLN expression in vasculature

claim: Both Ocln+/+ and OclnΔN/ΔN mice exhibited centrosomal staining with OCLN C-terminus antibody at E10.5 and E14.5 in the developing cortex.
source: In contrast, both Ocln+/+ and OclnΔN/ΔN mice exhibited centrosomal staining with OCLN C-terminus antibody (detects both mOCLN-FL and mOCLN-ΔN) at E10.5 and E14.5 in the developing cortex (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The mutant mice still express the shorter isoform mOCLN-ΔN but not mOCLN-FL.
source: Thus, the mutant mice still express the shorter isoform mOCLN-ΔN but not mOCLN-FL.
evidence: Inferred from immunohistochemistry and Western blot data

claim: mOCLN-ΔN only localizes at the centrosome and not at the plasma membrane.
source: These data are in agreement with subcellular fractionation results showing that mOCLN-ΔN only localizes at the centrosome and not at the plasma membrane (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 1D

claim: There is a significant 8–12% reduction in cortical surface area in OclnΔN/ΔN brains at P7 and P20.
source: As early as postnatal day 7 (P7) and persisting through P20, we observed a significant 8–12% reduction in cortical surface area in OclnΔN/ΔN brains (Figure 2E,F)
evidence: Supported by quantification of cortical area shown in Figure 2E,F

claim: There is a reduction in cortex thickness in OclnΔN/ΔN brains.
source: as well as a reduction in cortex thickness (Figure 2G,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification of cortical thickness shown in Figure 2G,H

claim: M-phase prolongation influences radial glial cell (RGC) division outcomes, leading to more apoptotic events and early cell cycle exit.
source: The first is M-phase prolongation, which has been shown to influence radial glial cell (RGC) division outcomes, leading to more apoptotic events and early cell cycle exit, generating neurons at the expense of the progenitor pool (Pilaz et al., 2016; Lizarraga et al., 2010; Marthiens et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: There is a significant increase in mitotic index in E10.5 and E12.5, but not E14.5 Ocln-mutant cortices compared to wild-type.
source: We observed a significant increase in mitotic index, defined as the number of PH3+ M-phase cells per total number of cells, in E10.5 and E12.5, but not E14.5 Ocln-mutant cortices compared to wild-type (Figure 3A,B)
evidence: Supported by quantification of mitotic index shown in Figure 3A,B

claim: There is a higher percentage of cells in OclnΔN/ΔN E12.5 cortices in prometaphase and metaphase (PM+M) compared to wild-type.
source: Furthermore, similar to previous reports of prolonged M-phase (Pilaz et al., 2016), we observed a higher percentage of cells in OclnΔN/ΔN E12.5 cortices in prometaphase and metaphase (PM+M) compared to wild-type (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of M-phase stages shown in Figure 3C,D

claim: There are significantly reduced numbers of Ki67-labeled, cycling cells in the E12.5 OclnΔN/ΔN mutant mice.
source: The increased mitotic index in the Ocln-mutant was not due to greater overall proliferation in the cortex since we observed significantly reduced numbers of Ki67-labeled, cycling cells in the E12.5 OclnΔN/ΔN mutant mice (Figure 3E,F)
evidence: Supported by quantification of Ki67+ cells shown in Figure 3E,F

claim: The increased mitotic index reflects a greater proportion of proliferative cells in M-phase.
source: indicating that the increased mitotic index reflects a greater proportion of proliferative cells in M-phase.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of increased mitotic index and reduced Ki67+ cells

claim: There is a critical period of mOCLN-FL function from the earliest cortical event of neural tube formation lasting until E12.5.
source: Taken together, these results point to a critical period of mOCLN-FL function, from the earliest cortical event of neural tube formation lasting until E12.5, as mOCLN-FL is downregulated, asymmetric divisions and the rate of neurogenesis increases (Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996).
evidence: Inferred from the timing of phenotypes and OCLN expression patterns

claim: Both E10.5 and E12.5 cortices, but not E14.5 cortices, revealed a higher percentage of activated (cleaved) caspase 3 (CC3)-positive apoptotic cells in mutant embryos compared to controls.
source: Both E10.5 and E12.5 cortices, but not E14.5 cortices, revealed a higher percentage of activated (cleaved) caspase 3 (CC3)-positive apoptotic cells in mutant embryos compared to controls (Figure 3G,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification of CC3+ cells shown in Figure 3G,H

claim: Delayed mitosis leads to more apoptotic events that are concurrent with time points (E10.5 and E12.5) in which mOCLN-FL should be expressed but is lost in Ocln-mutants.
source: Thus, delayed mitosis leads to more apoptotic events that are concurrent with time points (E10.5 and E12.5) in which mOCLN-FL should be expressed but is lost in Ocln-mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between timing of apoptosis and OCLN-FL expression

claim: OCLN knockdown in MDCK cells impaired mitotic cleavage angle of those dividing kidney epithelial cells.
source: Similar to OCLN knockdown in MDCK cells that impaired mitotic cleavage angle of those dividing kidney epithelial cells (Odenwald et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Mutant RGCs have skewed cleavage plane orientation compared to control.
source: we also observed skewed cleavage plane orientation (Pilaz et al., 2016; Jayaraman et al., 2016) in mutant RGCs compared to control (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by quantification of cleavage plane angle shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: Loss of mOCLN-FL expression impacts mitotic behavior, lengthening M-phase, and increasing apoptotic events prior to E14.5.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that loss of mOCLN-FL expression impacts mitotic behavior, lengthening M-phase, and increasing apoptotic events prior to E14.5.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on mitotic index, apoptosis, and OCLN expression

claim: At E12.5, there is an increase in TUJ1+ neurons and a reduction of PAX6+ RGCs in OclnΔN/ΔN compared to wild-type mice.
source: At E12.5, when the rate of neurogenesis normally rises (Haubensak et al., 2004; Huttner and Kosodo, 2005; Mione et al., 1997), we observed a further increase in TUJ1+ neurons and a reduction of PAX6+ RGCs in OclnΔN/ΔN compared to wild-type mice (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: The percentage of cycling intermediate progenitor cells (IPCs) dual-labeled with TBR2 and KI67 antibodies is greater in mutant cortices.
source: Furthermore, the percentage of cycling intermediate progenitor cells (IPCs) dual-labeled with TBR2 and KI67 antibodies is greater in mutant cortices, suggesting both the rates of symmetric neurogenic divisions and indirect neurogenic (IPC-generating) RGC divisions are increased at the expense of the RGC progenitor pool (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 4C,D

claim: The TUJ1+ cell layer was thicker in mutant compared to control cortices at E12.5.
source: Later in corticogenesis, although the TUJ1+ cell layer was thicker in mutant compared to control cortices at E12.5, by E16.5 Ocln mutant cortices displayed thinner TUJ1+ cortical layers
evidence: Supported by quantification of TUJ1+ layer width

claim: By E16.5 Ocln mutant cortices displayed thinner TUJ1+ cortical layers.
source: by E16.5 Ocln mutant cortices displayed thinner TUJ1+ cortical layers, indicating that precocious differentiation of neural progenitors at E12.5 leads to thinning of mutant cortex at later ages (Figure 4E,F).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 4E,F

claim: There is a significant reduction of both deep-layer CTIP2+ and superficial-layer CUX1+ cells in OclnΔN/ΔN cortex at P1.
source: Finally, we analyzed postnatal day 1 (P1) cortices for layer markers and found a significant reduction upon immunolabeling of both deep-layer CTIP2+ and superficial-layer CUX1+ cells in OclnΔN/ΔN cortex (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 4G,H

claim: Loss of mOCLN-FL in early corticogenesis leads to precocious neuronal differentiation, reducing cell output, contributing to cortex thinning by E16.5.
source: Together, these data indicate that loss of mOCLN-FL in early corticogenesis leads to precocious neuronal differentiation, reducing cell output, contributing to cortex thinning by E16.5.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on neuronal differentiation and cortex thickness

claim: Differences in progenitor characteristics, including the abundance of outer radial glial cells (oRG) in humans limits the ability of mouse models to recapitulate all aspects of human brain malformations.
source: However, differences in their progenitor characteristics, including the abundance of outer radial glial cells (oRG) in humans limits the ability of mouse models to recapitulate all aspects of human brain malformations (Lizarraga et al., 2010; Barrera et al., 2010; Pulvers et al., 2010; Gruber et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing was employed to interrupt OCLN in hESCs at exon 3.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 genome editing was employed to interrupt OCLN in hESCs at exon 3, the same exon targeted in the OclnΔN/ΔN mutant mouse (Saitou et al., 2000) and the location of half of the reported OCLN truncating mutations in patients (Abdel-Hamid et al., 2017; O'Driscoll et al., 2010; Jenkinson et al., 2018; Aggarwal et al., 2016; Elsaid et al., 2014).
evidence: Describes the experimental approach used in the study

claim: Half of the reported OCLN truncating mutations in patients are located at exon 3.
source: the same exon targeted in the OclnΔN/ΔN mutant mouse (Saitou et al., 2000) and the location of half of the reported OCLN truncating mutations in patients (Abdel-Hamid et al., 2017; O'Driscoll et al., 2010; Jenkinson et al., 2018; Aggarwal et al., 2016; Elsaid et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published patient mutation reports

claim: Six human OCLN (hOCLN) isoforms have been discovered to date.
source: Six human OCLN (hOCLN) isoforms have been discovered to date (Kohaar et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to published study

claim: Only four human OCLN isoforms have confirmed expression in the human brain.
source: although only four isoforms have confirmed expression in the human brain.
evidence: Based on published knowledge

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 targeting of exon 3 resulted in lost expression of all explored hOCLN isoforms except for hOCLN-ex3del.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 targeting of exon 3 resulted in lost expression of all explored hOCLN isoforms except for hOCLN-ex3del, as this isoform skips exon 3 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B

claim: No off-target mutations were observed in either sg5 or sg11 mutant hESC lines.
source: A list of potential off-target sites was obtained through http://chopchop.cbu.uib.no/ and each locus was sequenced in both wild-type and mutant cell lines. No off-target mutations were observed in either sg5 or sg11 mutant hESC lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2

claim: Full-length hOCLN (hOCLN-wt) can be found in both membrane and soluble nuclear fractions.
source: As in the mouse, full-length hOCLN (hOCLN-wt) can be found in both membrane and soluble nuclear fractions (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Endogenous hOCLN-ex4del localizes to both membrane and soluble fractions.
source: Endogenous hOCLN-ex4del, which is missing exon four and consequently lacks the fourth of its transmembrane domains, also localizes to both membrane and soluble fractions
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data

claim: hOCLN-ex3del was found only in the soluble nuclear fraction.
source: while the hOCLN-ex3del splice form, missing three of its four transmembrane domains, was found only in the soluble nuclear fraction.
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data

claim: Both sg5 and sg11 undifferentiated mutant lines have lost expression of hOCLN-wt and hOCLN-ex4del.
source: Immunocytochemical analysis using an N-terminus-specific OCLN antibody confirmed that both sg5 and sg11 undifferentiated mutant lines have lost expression of hOCLN-wt and hOCLN-ex4del, both normally expressed at the plasma membrane and at the centrosome (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 5D

claim: hOCLN-ex3del localized solely at the centrosome and remained expressed in sg5 and sg11 mutant lines.
source: However, hOCLN-ex3del localized solely at the centrosome and remained expressed in sg5 and sg11 mutant lines as shown by immunoreactivity with C-terminus OCLN antibody (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by immunocytochemistry data shown in Figure 5E

claim: There is ~40% and ~60% reductions in the circumferences of mutant organoids at d20 and d40, respectively.
source: We also saw ~40% and~60% reductions in the circumferences of mutant organoids at d20 and d40, respectively (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by quantification of organoid circumference shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: d10 mutant organoids have reduced proliferation and an increased mitotic index.
source: To explore the mechanisms underlying the size reduction, we assessed the proliferative capacity of d10 organoids and found reduced proliferation and an increased mitotic index in sg5 and sg11 mutant organoids (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 6C–E

claim: By d20, mutant lines exhibited increased apoptosis and increased TUJ1+ neuronal cell populations compared to controls.
source: By d20, mutant lines exhibited increased apoptosis and increased TUJ1+ neuronal cell populations compared to controls (Figure 6F–I).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 6F–I

claim: hOCLN-wt deficiency in this 3D human in vitro model mimics the mouse model with respect to prolonged M-phase, premature neuronal differentiation, and increased apoptosis.
source: These results suggest that hOCLN-wt deficiency in this 3D human in vitro model mimics the mouse model with respect to prolonged M-phase, premature neuronal differentiation, and increased apoptosis.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of organoid and mouse phenotypes

claim: The ratio of HOPX+/NeuroD1+ cell numbers was greatly reduced in the mutant organoids.
source: We therefore examined organoids by immunostaining for oRG marker, HOPX, compared to early neuronal marker NeuroD1. The ratio of HOPX+/NeuroD1+ cell numbers was greatly reduced in the mutant organoids (Figure 6J,K).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 6J,K

claim: Human OCLN is important for the balance between oRGs and neurons in the human cortex.
source: This suggests that human OCLN is important for the balance between oRGs and neurons in the human cortex and may explain the more pronounced deficit in human organoid size compared to the mild reduction in cortical size of the mouse.
evidence: Inferred from the oRG/neuron ratio data and comparison to mouse phenotype

claim: OCLN interacts with small GTPase nuclear protein RAN.
source: Among these candidates were small GTPase nuclear protein RAN, known for its role in nucleo-cytoplasmic transport and spindle assembly (Cavazza and Vernos, 2015; Carazo-Salas et al., 2001; Caudron et al., 2005; Li et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data

claim: OCLN interacts with NuMA.
source: and NuMA, a key player in spindle assembly and maintenance (Chu et al., 2016; Silk et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data

claim: There is a robust pulldown of both hOCLN-wt and hOCLN-ex3del isoforms by anti-NuMA antibody and reciprocal pulldown of NuMA by C-terminus OCLN antibody from hESC lysates.
source: We observed a robust pulldown of both hOCLN-wt and hOCLN-ex3del isoforms by anti-NuMA antibody and reciprocal pulldown of NuMA by C-terminus OCLN antibody (thus recognizing both hOCLN-wt and hOCLN-ex3del isoforms) from hESC lysates (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Co-localization of OCLN and NuMA was observed at the mitotic spindle poles during M-phase.
source: NuMA-OCLN interaction was further supported by immunostaining in which co-localization of both proteins was observed at the mitotic spindle poles during M-phase (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7B

claim: NuMA-labeled spindle pole morphology appeared rounded more frequently in sg5 and sg11 mutants.
source: NuMA-labeled spindle pole morphology appeared rounded more frequently in sg5 and sg11 mutants (Figure 7C–F), specifically exhibiting a circular shape rather than the expected elongated or half-moon shape of normal NuMA immunostaining (Nguyen and Munger, 2009).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 7C–F

claim: Both sg5 and sg11 mutant lines exhibited significantly weaker astral spindle labeling of alpha-tubulin, with shorter and fewer spindles, compared to control.
source: Since NuMA is known to be important to mitotic spindle stability and chromosome alignment (Chu et al., 2016; Silk et al., 2009) and has also been shown to regulate astral spindle orientation and tethering to the cell cortex (Seldin et al., 2016), we explored astral spindle morphology and showed that both sg5 and sg11 mutant lines exhibited significantly weaker astral spindle labeling of alpha-tubulin, with shorter and fewer spindles, compared to control (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 7G,H

claim: There is a higher frequency of altered mitotic spindle features such as abnormal spindle tilts and asymmetric spindle densities in sg5 and sg11 mutants compared to control.
source: Finally, we observed a higher frequency of altered mitotic spindle features such as abnormal spindle tilts and asymmetric spindle densities, higher frequency of chromosome misalignment, and reduced intensity of acetylated alpha-tubulin staining, in sg5 and sg11 mutants compared to control (Figure 7I–M).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 7I–M

claim: There is a higher frequency of chromosome misalignment in sg5 and sg11 mutants compared to control.
source: higher frequency of chromosome misalignment, and reduced intensity of acetylated alpha-tubulin staining, in sg5 and sg11 mutants compared to control (Figure 7I–M).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 7I–M

claim: There is reduced intensity of acetylated alpha-tubulin staining in sg5 and sg11 mutants compared to control.
source: and reduced intensity of acetylated alpha-tubulin staining, in sg5 and sg11 mutants compared to control (Figure 7I–M).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 7I–M

claim: The karyotype of wild-type undifferentiated hESCs was indistinguishable from that of undifferentiated hESC-sg5 or hESC-sg11 cells.
source: The karyotype of wild-type undifferentiated hESCs was indistinguishable from that of undifferentiated hESC-sg5 or hESC-sg11 cells.
evidence: Supported by karyotype analysis

claim: The frequency of one or more abnormal chromosomes per cell was significantly increased in sg5 and sg11 organoids compared to control organoids.
source: We therefore compared the karyotypes of metaphase cells from dissociated d20 WT, sg5, and sg11 3-D organoids (Figure 7—figure supplement 2). The frequency of one or more abnormal chromosomes per cell was significantly increased in sg5 and sg11 organoids compared to control organoids.
evidence: Supported by karyotype analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2

claim: Increased aneuploidy would be expected to contribute to the observed increase in apoptosis.
source: This would be expected to contribute to the observed increase in apoptosis and is consistent with the prolonged M-phase and cell death seen at E10.5 and E12.5 in the OclnΔN/ΔN mouse.
evidence: Inferred from the relationship between aneuploidy and apoptosis

claim: OCLN mediates spindle integrity and stability.
source: Together, these results provide compelling evidence for OCLN mediation of spindle integrity and stability.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data on OCLN interactions and spindle defects

claim: TJ proteins ZO-1 and ZO-2 were found to localize to the nucleus in vitro in a cell-confluency-dependent manner.
source: Indeed, TJ proteins ZO-1 and ZO-2 were found to localize to the nucleus in vitro in a cell-confluency-dependent manner (Gottardi et al., 1996; Jaramillo et al., 2004; Traweger et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published studies

claim: Previous proteomic studies found that nuclear envelope protein Emerin pulled-down with OCLN in vitro.
source: Furthermore, it is interesting that previous proteomic studies probing for OCLN-associated proteins found that nuclear envelope protein Emerin pulled-down with OCLN in vitro (Fredriksson et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to published proteomic study

claim: Prolonged mitosis of ventricular neural progenitors will alter division outcomes of RGCs, promoting neuronal differentiation and apoptosis at the expense of the progenitor pool and so lead to microcephaly.
source: One prominent mechanistic model of microcephaly proposes that prolonged mitosis of ventricular neural progenitors will alter division outcomes of RGCs, promoting neuronal differentiation and apoptosis at the expense of the progenitor pool and so lead to microcephaly (Pilaz et al., 2016; Lizarraga et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Mitosis is prolonged in both mouse OclnΔN/ΔN cortex and human 3-D organoids from two independent (sg5 and sg11) genome-edited hESC lines.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, our results indicate that mitosis is prolonged in both mouse OclnΔN/ΔN cortex and human 3-D organoids from two independent (sg5 and sg11) genome-edited hESC lines (Figures 4 and 6) and parallels the human microcephaly phenotype.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 4 and 6

claim: Loss of the hOCLN-wt, hOCLN-ex4del, and hOCLN-ex7ext isoforms in 3-D cultures resulted in premature neuronal differentiation at the expense of the progenitor pool.
source: Similar to the mouse data, loss of the hOCLN-wt, hOCLN-ex4del, and hOCLN-ex7ext isoforms in 3-D cultures resulted in premature neuronal differentiation at the expense of the progenitor pool.
evidence: Supported by organoid data

claim: HOPX+ oRGs constitute the majority of the human neural progenitor population.
source: Unlike the mouse, HOPX+ oRGs constitute the majority of the human neural progenitor population (LaMonica et al., 2012) and these were severely affected by OCLN loss in 3-D culture.
evidence: Supported by citation to published study and organoid data

claim: The paucity of oRG cells in rodents likely contributes to the significant but milder degree of microcephaly in the mouse compared to human patients.
source: The paucity of oRG cells in rodents likely contributes to the significant but milder degree of microcephaly in the mouse compared to human patients, who typically display occipital-frontal head circumferences at ~4 standard deviations below the mean or smaller.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in oRG abundance and severity of phenotypes

claim: The significant impact of OCLN mutations on mitotic spindle integrity, proliferation and survival are shown to be independent of potential deleterious effects from impaired vascular neogenesis, perivascular extravasation and calcification.
source: Importantly, since organoids lack vasculature and inflammatory cells, the significant impact of these OCLN mutations on mitotic spindle integrity, proliferation and survival are shown to be independent of potential deleterious effects from impaired vascular neogenesis, perivascular extravasation and calcification.
evidence: Inferred from the fact that organoids lack vasculature yet still show phenotypes

claim: Astral spindle abnormalities associated with loss of full-length OCLN are consistent with an earlier observation that perturbations in astral spindles by disruption of LGN limited their reach to the apical and basal regions of the cell's cortical actin meshwork, skewed the cleavage plane and increased the rate of asymmetric, neurogenic divisions of cortical progenitors.
source: Finally, our results link OCLN function with mitotic and astral spindle integrity, likely in part through its interactions with proteins like NuMA and RAN. In the present study, astral spindle abnormalities associated with loss of full-length OCLN are consistent with an earlier observation that perturbations in astral spindles by disruption of LGN limited their reach to the apical and basal regions of the cell's cortical actin meshwork, skewed the cleavage plane and increased the rate of asymmetric, neurogenic divisions of cortical progenitors (Mora-Bermúdez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published study and comparison to current findings

claim: Spindle protein LGN is a well-known interaction partner of NuMA.
source: Spindle protein LGN is a well-known interaction partner of NuMA (Du et al., 2001; Morin et al., 2007), which we show interacts with OCLN in neural progenitors.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: OCLN has a new role in neurogenesis and survival with a specific requirement for full-length OCLN in the promotion of early progenitor self-renewal through proper neural stem cell mitotic spindle function.
source: Together, these data illuminate a new role for OCLN in neurogenesis and survival with a specific requirement for full-length OCLN in the promotion of early progenitor self-renewal through proper neural stem cell mitotic spindle function.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data presented in the study
